The n-octanol saturated by water was used as organic phase, and water saturated by n-octanol was used as aqueous phase. Test chemical were weighted accurately to 0.0001 g and added into 25 mL volumetric flask. Then 15.0 mL of organic phase was added, and the flask was shaken to make chemicals dissolved sufficiently. Then we brought to volume by organic phase (the concentration of chemical was controlled as 0.008 mol/L). 10.0 mL of organic solution was brought in a 250 mL ground glass conical flask in which there is 40.0 mL aqueous phase, and then the stopper was plugged. The system was put into an oven controlled crystal oscillator and shaken at 25 °C. Octanol solutions of each compound at a different concentration (0.0008 mol/L) and three flasks for each concentration were prepared to validate the accuracy of the experiment. We tested the concentrations in aqueous phase after 24 h when the equilibrium was achieved. Blanks were prepared in an identical manner, with the exception that no compounds were added. The mixed solution was centrifuged, and the concentration of compounds in aqueous phase and organic phase were determined, respectively, using HPLC(Agilent 1620, USA). Measurements were made at 25 °C, on an Agilent Rx-C18 column (5 μm, 250 × 4.6 mm inner diameter), and analyses were detected with an Agilent1620 Series diode array detector. The mobile phases were mixtures of methanol and 0.5% of tetrafluorine acetic acid with volume ratio 75:25. A flow rate of 1.0 mL/min was adopted and the injection volume was 40 μL. The log P values were calculated as follows: log P = Cn-octanol/Cwater, where, Cn-octanol is the concentration of the test compound in n-octanol phase, Cwater is the concentration of the test compound in water phase.

Lipophilicity was determined as the partition coefficient between n-octanol and water (log P o/w) and as the chromatographic retention factor (log k w). The log P o/w determination was carried out according to the OECD guidelines for the classical shake flask method [23] with slight modifications. The complexes were dissolved in Milli-Q water (pre-saturated with 1-octanol) and the platinum concentration was determined by ICP-MS. The remaining stock solution was mixed with an equal volume of 1-octanol (pre-saturated with Milli-Q water) and shaken for 1 h. After phase separation, the platinum concentration was again determined in the aqueous phase by ICP-MS and the partition coefficients were calculated assuming the missing quantity (compared to the stock solution) in the organic phase. ICP-MS measurements were carried out after dilution of the samples with 1 % HNO3 using the instrumental parameters given in Table 1.

Weighted amounts of the tested platinum complex were suspended by 10 min sonification in 0.9% NaCl water solution, which was previously saturated with n-octanol, and mixed by shaking for 1 h. A simultaneously similar procedure was performed using 5 mL of n-octanol pre-saturated with 0.9% NaCl. Afterward, both suspensions were mixed together, shaken for an additional 1 h, and centrifuged for 5 min. After phase separation and evaporation in vacuo of 1 mL of sample to dryness, the final concentration of Pt was determined by ICP-OES (λ = 265.945 nm) and the partition coefficients were calculated. For the analysis, all samples were dissolved 1:1000 in 2.5% HCl. Each measurement was repeated four times and the final logP was calculated as the arithmetic mean of the four values. Directly after the experiment, all organic and water phases were tested (TLC) for their homogeneity, but no symptoms of decomposition or isomerization of Pt compounds were detected [45,46].

The cellular accumulation of a chemotherapeutic agent is often correlated with its lipophilicity, so we studied the lipophilicity (log D) of 3–6 by the shake-flask method in an octanol/water mixture (Fig. 5b). The lowest log D was observed for 3, while 6showed the highest log D value. Complexes 3–5 were more hydrophilic in the order of 3 > 4 > 5, whereas 6 was moderately lipophilic. This lipophilicity pattern does not correlate with higher cellular accumulation or better cytotoxicity. The cytotoxicity is the highest for 5 (oxamusplatin) and also 5 accumulates the most in cells, but it is more hydrophilic than 6. Complexes 3and 5 are quite different in terms of lipophilicity, yet they are more similar in terms of accumulation in cells. Complex 6 is a stable complex with lipophilicity within the range for better accumulation, but it shows lower accumulation in cells.

Partition coefficients of the platinum(IV) complexes were determined in an octanol/water system. Briefly, platinum complexes were dissolved and diluted to 50 μM in water. Equal volumes of the drug solution and n-octanol were shaken in vortex for 15 min, and after centrifugation (4000 rpm, 15 min) the platinum content in the aqueous layer was analyzed by ICP–AES (Model ELAN5000, Perkin Elmer, Norwalk, CT, USA). Partition coefficients were expressed as the log of the partition ratio of the total platinum in octanol to that in the aqueous layer.

The log Pow determination of DN604 was conducted by using the shake flask method. Excess DN604 was dissolved in KH2PO4/NaOH (0.1 M, pH 7.4) buffer solution presaturated with n-octanol for 48 h at 37 °C. The solution was filtered to remove undissolved platinum(II) compound. The initial concentration of platinum content was determined by RP-HPLC analysis. Subsequently, the platinum(II) solution was added to an equal volume of n-octanol (presaturated with KH2PO4/NaOH buffer for 48 h). The heterogeneous mixture was shaken vigorously for 2 h before centrifuging for 15 min to achieve phase separation. The final concentration of platinum content in the aqueous phase was again determined by RP-HPLC, and the water–octanol partition coefficient was calculated. In addition, all the aqueous solution was diluted 10 fold before HPLC study due to the high concentration. The experiment was performed in triplicate.

Solutions of complexes (50, 100, 150, 200 μm, respectively) were prepared in phosphate buffer (10 mm, pH 7.4) pre-saturated with 1-octanol. Equal volumes (2.0 mL) of the solution and 1-octanol pre-saturated with the phosphate buffer were mixed and placed in a thermostatic (25.0±0.1 °C) air bath orbital shaker at 200 rpm for 4 h. The samples were separated into two phases after centrifugation at 2500 rpm for 15 min. The concentration of the solute in the aqueous phase was determined by spectrophotometry (λmax=267 nm). According to the law of mass conservation, the drug concentration of the 1-octanol phase and the lipo-hydro partition coefficient PO/W (PO/W=CO/CW=AO/AW, A stands for absorbance) were calculated. The average of three parallel experimental data was reported as the final result.

Partition coefficients for the platinum complexes were determined in duplicate in an n-octanol/water system. Each complex was dissolved in n-octanol at 2 × 10-5 M and subsequently an equal volume of water was added. The mixtures were shaken mechanically for 24 h to ensure the distribution between the two solvent phases. The samples were centrifuged (13,000 rpm, 5 min) Afterwards they were diluted 5-fold and the platinum concentration was determined in both phases by GFAAS in a Varian model Zeeman 220 spectrophotometer equipped with a graphite tube atomizer and an autosampler. Results are expressed as apparent partition coefficients (P), which is the total platinum in n-octanol divided by the total platinum in the aqueous layer [14].

Log P values of these compounds were determined using a shake-flask method [66]. Aqueous sodium chloride (0.9% w/v) and 1-octanol (99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich) phases were saturated for 1 week. In case of 1-mat and 2-mat derivatives weighed amounts of platinum complexes (1–2 mg) were dissolved in the aqueous phase (10 mL) and an equal volume of saturated 1-octanol was added. Alternatively, weighed amounts of 1-pat and 2-tbat platinum complexes (1–2 mg) were dissolved in 10 mL of 1-octanol and an equal volume of aqueous phase was added. The resulting solutions were mixed for 1 h. Samples were filtered and platinum content of the aqueous phases determined by atomic absorption spectroscopy (k = 265.9 nm) using Carl Zeiss 30 AAS apparatus. The experiments were performed in triplicate. Platinum content of 1-octanol phase was calculated as a difference between concentrations before and after mixing of the phases. The logarithm of the ratio of platinum concentrations in the organic and aqueous phases was calculated to determine log P values reported in Table 3.

Octanol-saturated water (OSW) and water-saturated octanol (WSO) were prepared from octanol and distilled water (overnight shaking; Vibramax 100, Heidolph Instruments). The stock solutions of 2, 4 and cisplatin were prepared as follows: complexes (1 mg) were ultrasonicated in 15 mL of OSW for 15 min, centrifuged and supernatants were collected. Octanol-saturated water (OSW) and water-saturated octanol (WSO) were prepared from octanol and 0.2 M water solution of KI by overnight stirring. The stock solutions were prepared by shaking of 1 μmol of 1 and 2 in 11 mL of OSW for 1 h. Then the mixtures were centrifuged (5 min, 11,000 rpm) and the supernatant was collected. 5 mL of this solution was studied by ICP-MS (to assess [M]OSWb as the Pt concentration before the partition), while another 5 mL of this solution was added to 5 mL of WSO and shaken at ambient temperature for 2 h. After that, these mixtures were centrifuged, and the aqueous layers were carefully separated. The Pt concentrations were determined by ICP-MS (the obtained value was corrected for the adsorption effects). The equation log P = log([M]WSO/[M]OSWa) was used for the partition coefficient calculation, where [M]OSWa stands for the Pt concentration after partition, and [M]WSO = [M]OSWb - [M]OSWa. The experiment was conducted in triplicate and the results are presented as arithmetic mean ± SD.

The n-octanol/water partition coefficient logP was determined by the “shake flask” method. Equal amounts of PBS buffer (10 mM, pH 7.4) and n-octanol were mixed in a conical flask and then stirred for 72 h, followed by separation of the two phases. Then, stock solutions of the metal complexes (approx. 1 mg in 200 μL of solvent) were prepared in DMSO and 10 μL thereof mixed with 750 μL of either the water or octanol phase. After mixing on a vortexer for 15 min, the vials were centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 5 min, the two phases separated and the absorbance measured on an Agilent 8453 UV/Vis diode array spectrophotometer. LogP values were then calculated using eq. 1: logP = log(A_octanol(300 nm) / A_PBS(300 nm))

Octanol-saturated water (OSW) and water-saturated octanol (WSO) were prepared from n-octanol and 0.2 M water solution of KI by the overnight stirring. Stock solutions were prepared by ultrasonication (5 min) and shaking (30 min) of 1 µmol of complexes 1–4 in 20 mL of OSW. After that, the mixtures were centrifuged (5 min, 11,000 rpm) and supernatants were collected. 5 mL of this solution was added to 5 mL of WSO and shaken at ambient temperature for 2 h. After that, the mixture was centrifuged and aqueous layer was separated carefully and the Pt concentration was determined by ICP-MS (the obtained value was corrected for the adsorption effects). logP = log([Pt]WSO/[Pt]OSWa) equation was used for the partition coefficient calculation; [Pt]OSWb and [Pt]OSWa stands for the Pt concentration before and after partition, respectively, and [Pt]WSO = [Pt]OSWb–[Pt]OSWa.

Partition coefficients of the platinum(II) complexes were determined in the octanol/water system. Briefly, platinum complexes were dissolved and diluted to 50 μM in water. Equal volumes of the drug solution and n-octanol were shaken in vortex for 15 min, and after centrifugation (4000 rpm for 15 min) the platinum content in the aqueous layers was analyzed by ICP-AES. The partition coefficient (P) is expressed as P=[Pt]o/[Pt]w, where [Pt]o and [Pt]w represent the total concentrations of the complex in the n-octanol and water layers, respectively, and the lipophilicity may be defined as its log function (log P). Thus the measured lipophilicities of the platinum(II) complexes are listed in Table 1. The lipophilicity of the complexes was plotted against the number of carbon atoms (n) of the N-substituents of the amino acids in Fig. 2. The n values of complexes 1–4 are 2, 3, 5 and 8, respectively, which are corresponding to the number of carbon atoms of Ac, Pro, Piv and Cbz groups, respectively.

To obtain octanol-saturated water and water-saturated octanol, 100 mL of PBS was stirred with 100 mL of octanol for 24 h, followed by centrifugation for 5 min. The platinum complexes were dissolved in 1.0 mL of octanol-saturated PBS to a typical concentration of 0.1 mM and then mixed with 1.0 mL water-saturated octanol. Triplicates of each experiment were mixed in a multi-tube vortexer incubator for 16 h at room temperature and then centrifuged for 5 min. The layers were separated carefully, and the content of platinum–acridines was determined spectrophotometrically at 413 nm (with ε413=10 000 M-1 cm-1 in octanol-saturated PBS and ε413=8600 M-1 cm-1 in PBS-saturated octanol). The partition coefficients (D) of the samples were then determined as the quotient of the concentration of compound in octanol and the concentration in the aqueous layer. Reported logD values are the mean ±standard deviations of three determinations.

The log Po/w values of Pt-DHA and Pt-BisDHA were determined using the shake-flask method. n-octanol and PBS buffer were added into a beaker, and the two-phase mixture was stirred at 25 °C for 24 h to obtain PBS-saturated octanol and octanol-saturated PBS. Then, 4.0 mg Pt-DHA or Pt-BisDHA was dissolved in 2.0 mL PBS-saturated octanol. The solution was filtered using a 0.22-μm syringe filter, and a small fraction of filtrate was taken out to measure the Pt content (marked as C(total)) using ICP-MS. Next, 1.0 mL of the remaining filtrate was mixed with 1.0 mL of octanol-saturated PBS in a tube. The tube was shaken at 25 °C in darkness for 24 h. Finally, the two phases were separated by centrifugation (8000 rpm, 60 min), and the Pt content (marked as C(PBS)) in the PBS phase was determined by ICP-MS. All the experiments were carried out in triplicate. The log Po/w value was calculated using the equation below. log𝑃𝑜/𝑤=log[(𝐶(total)-𝐶(PBS))/𝐶(PBS)]

The log P values were calculated from an average of three independent measurements.

The logP values of the Pt(IV) compounds were determined using the shake flask method55. The respective Pt(IV) complex was dissolved in 0.9% NaCl (w/v) ultrapure water (presaturated with n-octanol). The solutions were sonicated and filtered to remove undissolved Pt(IV) compounds. The initial Pt concentrations were determined by ICP-MS. Subsequently, the Pt(IV) solutions were added to an equal volume of n-octanol (presaturated with 0.9% NaCl (w/v) ultrapure water). The heterogeneous mixtures were shaken vigorously for 30 min before centrifuging at 4000 rpm for 30 min to achieve phase separation. The final Pt concentration in the aqueous phase was determined again by ICP-MS. The logarithm of the ratio of Pt concentrations in the organic and aqueous phases was calculated to determine the logP values.

The partition coefficients (P) of the investigated platinum complexes were determined by the “shake flask” method. The complexes were dissolved in octanol-saturated water (OSW) containing 200 mm NaCl and mixed with water-saturated octanol (WSO) in volumetric ratios of 2:1, 1:1, and 1:2. Mixing was done by vortexing for 30 min at room temperature to establish the partition equilibrium. To separate the phases, centrifugation was done at 3000 g for 5 min. The layers were separated carefully by using a fine-tip pipette and then analyzed for metal content by flameless atomic absorption spectroscopy (FAAS). The partition coefficients were calculated as the ratio of the concentration of the compound in the octanol layer to that in the aqueous layer, log P=log ([Pt]WSO/[Pt]OSW).

The partition coefficient was determined from the solubilization of 1 mg of the compound in 300 μL of DMSO. Then, 30 μL of the solution was transferred to a microtube, 750 µL of n-octanol was added, and homogenized. Subsequently, 750 µL of water was added, and the resulting solutions were kept under stirring at 37 °C for 24 h [13]. The absorbance measurements of the complexes in n-octanol/water were performed in triplicate on a SHIMADZU UV-1650PC spectrophotometer. Considering the average absorbance obtained, the concentration value of the complexes in n-octanol and water were determined from the standard curve previously obtained. The standard curve was derived from obtaining spectra after eight successive additions of 50 μL of the solution of the complex in n-octanol into a cuvette containing 2500 μL containing n-octanol. The measure of lipophilicity adopted is the log P, which is the fraction between the concentration of the compound in n-octanol and water, as represented by the equation below: log P = [Compound]n-Oc/[Compound]water [14].

The logPo/w values of the Pt(IV) complexes were determined by the shake flask method.58 The respective Pt(IV) complex was dissolved in ultrapure water, presaturated with n-octanol, containing 0.9% NaCl (w/v). The solution was sonicated and undissolved Pt(IV) complex was removed. The Pt concentration was determined by ICP-MS. Then, the Pt(IV) solution was added to an equal volume of n-octanol, presaturated with 0.9% NaCl (w/v) in ultrapure water. After vigorous shaking for 30 min, the mixture was centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 30 min to achieve phase separation. The Pt concentration in the aqueous phase was analyzed by ICP-MS. The logPo/w value was calculated as the logarithm of the ratio of Pt concentrations in the organic and aqueous phases.

Octanol-water partition coefficients (log Po/w) of the Pt(IV) compounds were determined by the shake flask method [45]. All experiments were done in duplicate. The respective Pt(IV) complex was mixed with 0.9% NaCl (w/v) in ultrapure water that was presaturated with n-octanol for 3 d. All solutions were sonicated and filtered to remove undissolved Pt(IV) compound. The initial Pt concentrations were measured by ICP-MS (ELAN DRCe, Perkin Elmer, Waltham, USA) as described above. Subsequently, the Pt(IV) solution was added to an equal volume of n-octanol that was presaturated with 0.9% NaCl (w/v) in ultrapure water. The heterogeneous mixture was shaken vigorously for 1 h before centrifuging at 4400 rpm for 1 h to achieve phase separation. The final Pt concentration in the aqueous phase was measured again by ICP-MS. Log Po/w values were calculated as the ratio of Pt concentrations in the organic and aqueous phases.

The log Po/w values of all the carbonate and carboxylate complexes were measured by using a shake-flask method. The presaturated PBS and octanol utilized here were prepared by mixing the two-phase solution and then shaking at room temperature overnight. A portion of 0.5 mL of pre-saturated PBS buffer containing 50 μM Pt(IV) complex was incubated with the pre-saturated octanol (0.5 mL) in a 2 mL tube. The tube containing the two-phase mixtures was shaken at room temperature for 1 h. The two-phase mixtures were isolated by centrifugation and the platinum content in each phase was determined by ICP-OES. The results of log Po/w were expressed as a mean of three independent measurements.

Drugs were dissolved at a concentration of 0.30 mg mL-1 in 2.5 mL of saturated n-octanol, except cisplatin was dissolved in the aqueous phase. After separation, the phases were analyzed by UV–vis spectroscopy to determine the amount of compound in each phase. The procedures were repeated five times.

Shake-flask method was used to measure the partition coefficient for CDDP, 1 and 2. Briefly, a mixture of an equal volume of noctanol and phosphate buffer (10 mM, pH 7.4) was shaken on a mechanical shaker at room temperature for 24 h. Saturated solutions of the complexes in phosphate buffer (presaturated with n-octanol) were prepared in an ultrasonic bath followed by a filtration through a 0.2 µm nylon filter. Equal volumes of the solution and n-octanol presaturated with phosphate buffer were mixed and the mixtures were shaken for 24 h at room temperature. Centrifugation was carried out at 2500 rpm for 30 min to separate the two phases. The aqueous layer was carefully separated and the Pt content in initial and final aqueous phases was analyzed by ICP-MS. The log PO/W was measured using the following equation: log PO/W = log [(Ptinitial - Ptfinal)/Ptfinal].

The traditional octanol-water shake-flask method was used to detected the log Po/w values of compounds 1–8. First, n-octanol and PBS were shaken at 37 °C for 48 h to saturate each other, and then separated by separator funnel. Then, the standard curves of concentration-absorbance of compounds in two phases were established by UV spectrophotometer. The complexes 1-8 were dissolved in an equal volume mixture of mutually saturated n-octanol and PBS as described above, respectively, and then stirred in the dark for 24 h at 37 °C. The two phases were separated and determined by UV spectrophotometer, and the concentration in n-octanol (Co) and in PBS (Cw) was obtained ac-cording to the standard curves. The log P were obtained according the formula: log Po/w= log Co/Cw.

The log P values for compounds 1–6 were determined using the shake-flask method. Octanol-saturated water (OSW) and water-saturated octanol (WSO) were prepared by shaking a 1:1 mixture of 1-octanol and water for 24 h, followed by separation of each layer using a separating funnel. Stock solutions of 1–6 (ca. 2 mM) were made in DMSO, and 25 μL was added to 2 mL of WSO containing 100 mM NaCl. 600 μL of this solution was added to 600 μL of OSW in a 2 mL tube and shaken for 2 h at 37 °C using an automated shaker (800 rpm). 600 μL of this solution was added to 600 μL of OSW and stirred for 2 h at 37 °C at 800 rpm. The aqueous layer was carefully separated from the octanol layer. The Ru content, [Ru], was quantified in aqueous layers before and after partition using ICP–MS. log P was calculated using the following equation. log P = log( ([Ru]water_before_partition - [Ru]water_after_partition) / [Ru]water_after_partition )

Equal volumes of octanol and pure water were mixed and shaken for 24 h to pre-saturate the solutions. Equal volumes of the pre-treated octanol and water were then mixed, and the target compounds were added until saturation. The mixture was shaken for 48 h and centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 15 min. The Log Po/w values of the synthesized prodrugs were determined by measuring the UV absorbance of the compounds in the octanol and water phases at room temperature using a UV spectrophotometer. The log Pow was calculated using the formula (4-1), where Ao is the UV absorbance of the compound in octanol at a specific wavelength(273 nm), and Aw is the UV absorbance of the compound in the aqueous phase at the same wavelength(273 nm).

Solutions of AC and ACPt (50 μM) were prepared in the phosphate buffer (10 mM, pH 7.4) presaturated with 1-octanol. Partition coefficient is a parameter that determines how a solute substance is distributed between two phases, i.e., polar and nonpolar phases. In partition coefficient experiment, the polar phase is considered to be water and nonpolar phase is n-octanol which has two heads: (i) a long lipophilic alkyl chain (R) and (ii) a polar hydroxyl (OH) group. This structure of n-octanol resembles the lipid molecules (phospholipids and sterols) of cell membrane. So, octanol–water partition coefficient (log P) best represents the tendency of a given compound such as drug to pass across the cell membrane. In this study, the log P of [Pd(1, 3-pn)(acac)]Cl complex was measured by a shake-flask technique in a mixture of doubly distilled water and n-octanol (Manojkumar et al. 2019). Palladium(II) complex (0.002 g) was dissolved in a mixture of doubly distilled water and n-octanol (5 mL of each) and shaken without interruption overnight. It was then allowed to stand (without stirring) for one hour until phase separation occurred. After, the water and octanol phases were carefully separated with two different syringes. UV–Vis spectroscopy and Beer-Lambert law were utilized to determine the metal complex concentration in each phase. Eventually, the following equation was used to estimate the lipophilicity (log P) value of [Pd(1, 3-pn)(acac)]Cl complex: logP = log(Co/Cw), where CO and CW are the concentrations of complex in the octanol and aqueous phases, respectively.

Water or phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was stirred with octanol for 24 h, and then the mixture was centrifuged for 5 min to obtain octanol-saturated water and water-saturated octanol. 1–3 were dissolved in the octanol-saturated water (or PBS for cisplatin) at a typical concentration of 0.05 to 5 mM, and then they were mixed with water-saturated octanol in volumetric ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 2:1. All mixtures were prepared in duplicate. The mixtures were vortexed for 0.5 h, and then they were centrifuged for 5 min. The layers were separated carefully using a fine-gauge needle. The Pd content in the layers was analyzed by graphite furnace atomic absorption spectroscopy (GFAAS). The partition coefficient was taken as the ratio of the concentration of Pd in the octanol layer to that in the aqueous layer (P = coct/cwater). The reported error is the standard deviation of six measurements obtained according to this protocol.

The lipophilicity value of the Pd (II) complex was determined utilizing “shake flask” method in a blend of deionized water and n-octanol media [20]. At first, [Pd(bpy)(acac)]NO3 (0.001 g) was dissolved in a blend of water-octanol (10 mL, 1:1v/v) via shaking for 12 h. The lipophilicity of metal-based drugs was determined by shaking bottle technique. The specific operation is as follows: first, the two liquid phases of octanol and water are mutually saturated; Secondly, appropriate amount of complex (0.2 mg) was added to the centrifugal tube, and 2 mL of pre-saturated two-phase solution was added to the centrifugal tube respectively. Thirdly, the mixture containing the complex was vibrated on a shaker for 24 h and left to stand overnight. Two phases of water and octanol were carefully separated into test tubes, and 50 μL of each phase substance was dissolved in 1000 μL HNO3, and then diluted with distilled water. The rhodium or palladium analysis was determined by ICP-MS. These procedures were carried out at ambient temperature (298 K). Partition coefficients of complexes were calculated using the equation log P=log([Metal]octanol /[Metal]aqueous), (Metal stands for rhodium or palladium).

The lipophilicity of the complexes was determined by the “shake flask” method using a pH 7.4 phosphate buffer (0.129 M NaCl) and n-octanol as solvents.37 Each compound was dissolved in the phase in which it is most soluble, resulting in typical concentrations of 50 to 350 mM. Fifty rotations were performed by hand followed by one hour of settling time. Equilibration and absorption measurements were made at 20 ◦C.

The n-octanol–water partition coefficient was measured by using the shake-flask method.100 Distilled water and n-octanol were stirred together for 72 h at 25 °C, to promote saturation of both phases. The solvents were separated and freshly used. Aliquots of stock solutions (1.5 mM) of 1 and (150 μM) of 2 in the n-octanol saturated aqueous phase were added to equal volumes of water-saturated n-octanol and shaken on a mechanical shaker for 1 h. The resultant biphasic solution was centrifuged to separate the layers, and the UV/Vis absorption spectra of both solutions were recorded in both phases in a PerkinElmer Lambda 35 UV/Vis spectrophotometer at 372 nm (1) and 270 nm (2) and compared with a calibration curve to obtain the compound concentration of 1 and 2 in both phases. log P was defined as the logarithm of the ratio [Pd]octanol/[Pd] water or [Pt]octanol/[Pt]water, respectively; values reported are the means of three separate experiments.

The log P value was determined by using the “shake flask” method. Octanol was used as the organic phase, and water was employed as the aqueous phase. The analyzed complex was solubilized in 150 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide, partitioned into three tubes containing 50 μL of the solvent each. Then, 975 μL of n-octanol and 975 μL of water were added, which was followed by stirring at 1000 rpm and 296 K for 24 h. The phases were separated, and the concentration of the complex in the organic phase was determined by UV-Vis spectroscopy, by using a calibration curve previously prepared for the complex, in dimethyl sulfoxide. The log P value was calculated by applying eqn (1): log P = log(Co/Ca) where Co and Ca are the molar concentrations of the complex in the organic and aqueous phase, respectively; Ca can be obtained by subtracting the initial concentration of the complex in the organic phase from Co.

Partition coefficients (Pow; IUPAC: KD partition constant), defined as Pow = corg/caq, where corg and caq are molar concentrations of the selected compound in the organic and aqueous phase, respectively, were determined by the shake-flask method and UV/Vis measurements. Deionized water and octan-1-ol were vigorously stirred for 24 h, to enable saturation of both phases, then separated by centrifugation. A stock solution of the selected Fe compound (ca. 2 mg) was prepared by first adding acetone (50 μL, to help solubilization), followed by water-saturated octanol (2.5 mL). The solution was diluted with water-saturated octanol (ca. 1:3 v/v ratio, cFe2 ≈ 10⁻⁴ M, so that 1.5 ≤ A ≤ 2.0 at λmax) and its UV/Vis spectrum was recorded (A0org). An aliquot of the solution (Vorg = 1.2 mL) was transferred into a test tube and octanol-saturated water (Vorg = Vaq = 1.2 mL) was added. The mixture was vigorously stirred for 30 min at 21 °C then centrifuged (RCF 805, 5 min; Hettich EBA 8G). The UV/Vis spectrum of the organic phase was recorded (Aforg) and the partition coefficient was calculated as: Pow = Aforg / (A0org - Aforg) where A0org and Aforg are the absorbance in the organic phase before and after partition with the aqueous phase, respectively. For [2B]BF4, [2C]Cl and [3F]CF3SO3 an inverse procedure was followed, starting from a solution of the compound in octanol-saturated water. The partition coefficient was calculated as: Pow = (A0aq - Afaq) / Afaq where A0aq and Afaq are the absorbance in the aqueous phase before and after partition with the organic phase, respectively. The wavelength of the maximum absorption of each compound (320–390 nm range) was used for UV/Vis quantitation. The procedure was repeated three times for each sample (from the same stock solution); results are given as mean ± standard deviation (Table 3). Naphthoquinone was used as a reference compound (log P = 1.8 ± 0.2; literature: 1.71).

Distribution coefficients (D7.40) of the compounds were determined by the traditional shake-flask method in n-octanol/buffered aqueous solution at pH = 7.40 phosphate buffer saline (PBS) at 25.0 ± 0.2 °C. Compounds, except for quinH2, were dissolved in n-octanol pre-saturated buffered aqueous phase, and final compound concentration was 20–100 μM. Ligand quinH2 was dissolved in n-octanol pre-saturated by water in 2 mM concentration. Aqueous buffered phases and water pre-saturated n-octanolic phases were gently mixed in 1:1, 1:70 (for 3, 4), or 20:1 (for quinH2) volume ratios with Heidolph Reax 2 overhead shaker (~20 rpm) for 2 h. The mixtures were centrifuged with Eppendorf MiniSpin Plus centrifuge (5000 rpm, 3 min). After phase separation, UV-Vis spectrum of the compound in the aqueous phase (in the n-octanolic phase in case of quinH2) was compared to that of the original stock solution and DpH values of the compounds were calculated according to the following equations: DpH = [(Absstock solution / Absaqueous phase after separation) - 1] × (Vaqueous phase / Vn-octanol phase). A Hewlett Packard 8452a diode array spectrophotometer was used to measure the UV–Vis spectra in the interval 200–500 nm.

After allowing 30 min for the mixture to settle, the resulting two phases were collected separately without cross contamination of one solvent layer by another. By using UV-Vis absorption spectroscopy, the concentration of the cobalt(III) complex in each phase was determined and three independent experiments were performed so as to present the results as the mean values. The hydrophobicity values of cobalt(III) complexes (1–4) were compared in terms of partition coefficient (log P) values using the following equation: logP = log([Complex]octanol / [Complex]water)

Lipophilicity of the Pd(II) complex has been evaluated via “shake flask” procedure utilizing n-octanol/deionized water phase partition [30]. Proper amount of the Pd(II) complex (0.001 g/10 mL) was diluted in 10 mL blend of n-octanol and deionized water in equal volume (1:1 V/V) and shaken continuously for 24 h. After achieving the equilibrium condition, organic (n-octanol) and aqueous (deionized water) phases were carefully separated. Ultimately, the concentration of the metal complex in each separated phase was determined via electronic absorption spectroscopy and utilized to calculate log P (partition coefficient) using the equation log P = log ([Pd]in octanol/[Pd]in aqueous).

The final absorbance of the aqueous phase at the λmax of each compound was determined, and their water–octanol partition coefficient was calculated. All experiments were performed in triplicate.

Lipophilicity of complexes 1–6 were measured by determining their partition coefficients (logP) between n-octanol and water using the shake-flask method.1 First, an absorbance calibration plot was constructed for the complex at varying concentrations of the complex in the aqueous medium. Then, known concentration of the aqueous solution of the complex was mixed with equal volume of n-octanol. After vortex-shaking the mixture, the two phases were allowed to separate. The remaining concentration of the complex in aqueous phase was then determined from the calibration plot. The partition coefficient was calculated by using the equation logP = log[complex]oct/[complex]aq, where [complex]oct is the concentration of the complex in n-octanol phase and [complex]aq is the concentration in the aqueous phase.

A modified “shake-flask” method was employed to determine the partition coefficients (expressed as logP) of the complexes 1–5 between n-octanol and water following literature procedure [44]. Briefly, a 4 mL solution of the complexes (15, 20 and 25 μM) in n-octanol saturated water was added with 4 mL of water saturated n-octanol and mixed thoroughly in a vortex mixture for ∼ 20 min. The partition coefficients were calculated using the equation logP = log{[1–5]oct/[1–5]aq}. LogP was calculated as average of three different complex concentrations.

The water/1-octanol distribution coefficient, often represented as log P (logarithm of the partition coefficient), is a measure of how a compound distributes between water and 1-octanol. It is commonly used in medicinal and pharmaceutical chemistry to assess a compound's lipophilicity and its potential to cross biological membranes. Water–octanol partition coefficients were determined using the stir flask method [44]. A total of 1.0 mg of each complex is solubilized in 100 μL of DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide). The dilution: The DMSO solution containing the complex is diluted in a mixture of equal volumes of water (750 μL) and 1-octanol (750 μL). This results in the formation of a two-phase system, with the water and 1-octanol layers. The solutions are continuously shaken for 24 h at 1000 rpm and 37 °C. The agitation helps in achieving equilibrium between the water and 1-octanol phases. After the 24-hour shaking period, the samples are centrifuged for 5 min at 300 rpm. This step separates the two phases: the organic (1-octanol) phase and the aqueous (water) phase. The concentration of the complex in each phase (organic and aqueous) is measured spectrophotometrically. This measurement allows you to determine the concentration of the complex in both phases. The log P value is calculated as the ratio of the concentration of the complex in 1-octanol to the concentration of the complex in water. This ratio is expressed as Log P = [complex in 1-octanol]/[complex in water]. The entire experiment is carried out in triplicate, which means the whole process is repeated three times for each complex to ensure the reliability of the results.

The shake-flask method was used to measure the distribution coefficients (D) of the complexes in n-octanol/PBS pH = 7.40 at RT. PBS and n-octanol were mutually pre-saturated 1 week prior to use and separated. The complexes were dissolved in pre-saturated PBS solution to a concentration of ~100 μM. The resulting solutions were premixed with pre-saturated n-octanol for 72 h. The UV–Vis spectra of complexes in the aqueous phase were recorded. The aqueous solutions were mixed with pre-saturated n-octanol at a 1:10 volume ratio for 24 h. After phase separation, the UV–Vis spectra of the complexes in the aqueous phase were compared to that of the original solutions and the corresponding D values were calculated according to the following equation: D = [(Aaqueous phase before separation / Aaqueous phase after separation) - 1] × (Vaqueous phase / Voctanol phase). The UV–Vis spectra were recorded in the interval 250–600 nm using a Perkin Elmer Lambda 25 UV/Vis type spectrophotometer. Phase separation was done using a Scanspeed 406 centrifuge (Labogene, Lynga, Denmark) at 4000 rpm for 5 min.

The apparent octanol/water partition coefficients (log Pow) were determined using 50 mM NaCl/5 mM Tris, pH 7.2 buffer as the water phase. Briefly, the octanol was pre-saturated with the buffer for more than 24 h before use. A 24.8 μL aliquot of the compounds (of known pre-evaluated concentration), dissolved in octanol, was added to three different ratios of octanol/water buffer for a total volume of 12 mL. The samples were placed on a shaker for 6 h at 37 °C. After shaking, the samples were centrifuged for 5 min at 13,000g on a table-top microcentrifuge. The organic and the water phase were then analyzed by means of UV-spectrometry in order to determine the concentration of the examined compound in each of them. The ratio of concentrations in octanol versus buffered water phase was determined for each sample. The ratios were then averaged for the three different octanol/water buffer ratios used for each compound to calculate the partition coefficient.

The lipophilicity of the complexes was measured by determining their partition coefficients (logPo/w) between n-octanol (o) and water (w) using the shake-flask method.[49] The complexeswere dissolved in water containing 1% DMSO. A calibration plot for the complex wasconstructed by determining the absorbances by varying concentrations of the complex in theaqueous medium. The remaining concentration of the complex in the aqueous phasewas then determined from the calibration plot. The partition coefficient was calculated by usingthe equation log Po/w = log[C]o/[C]w, where [C]o is the concentration of the complex in the n-octanol phase and [C]w is the concentration in the water phase.

This experiment was performed following published literature. (29) Manganese(II) complex (1 mg) was dissolved in 2 mL of a 1:1 mixture of water and 1-octanol. The solution was shaken for 30 s, then the vial containing the mixture was placed on a rotator for gentle mixing to equilibrate for 48 h. The sample was then allowed to settle at room temperature for 24 h. Mn(II) concentrations of each layer were determined by ICP-MS (inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry). Partition coefficients were calculated from the equation log P = log(Co/Cw), where log P is the logarithm of the partition coefficient, Co is the concentration of Mn in the 1-octanol layer, and Cw is the concentration of Mn in the water layer.

Partition coefficients were measured at 25 °C. Briefly, water (5 mL) saturated with 1-octanol was added to each vial containing weighted amounts of a manganese(II) complex. Then 1 mL of each of these preparative solutions was pipetted into three cuvettes. To each cuvette, 1-octanol (9 mL) saturated with water was added. These solutions were then stoppered and shaken for 3 h, set aside to allow the two phases to separate at 25 °C. Concentrations of manganese(II) complexes in the aqueous phase before (C0) and after partitioning (Cw) were evaluated by spectrophotometry using the pyridyl ring bands (259 nm) of ligands. Based on the concentration ratio of each complex between 1-octanol and water phase, the partition coefficients were calculated as Kow = (C0V0 - CwVw) / CwVw.

The partition coefficient log P was determined by the ‘‘shakeflask’’ method. Briefly, equal volumes of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, 0.01 M, pH 7.4) and n-octanol were mixed, shaken together on a lab shaker (IKA KS 130 basic) for 72 and the phases then separated. Then, approx. 1 mg of each metal complex was dissolved in 300 mL of dimethyl sulfoxide with shaking. The n-octanol/water partition coefficient of compounds 4–7 was determined using the shake-flask method. PBS-buffered doubly distilled water [100 mL, phosphate buffer, [PO43–] = 10 mM, [NaCl] = 15 M, pH adjusted to 7.4 with hydrochloric acid] and n-octanol (100 mL) were shaken together using a laboratory shaker (Perkin–Elmer) for 72 h to allow saturation of both phases. In order to assess the potential relation between the hydrophobicity/lipophilicity of complexes and biological activity, partition coefficients (log Po/w) were determined in an octanol–water medium. Using the “shake flask” method, log Po/w values were calculated by assessing the ratio of equilibrium concentration between the n-octanol (organic) and water (aqueous) phase. The log Po/w values show that complex 1 has a value of 1.24 ± 0.04, complex 2 has 1.13 ± 0.02, and complex 3 has 1.01 ± 0.05, indicating that complexes 1 and 2 are more hydrophobic than complex 3. They follow the trend in the order of 1 > 2 > 3, and this difference likely results from the thiophene group present in the ligand backbone of complexes 1 and 2, which increases their hydrophobic nature compared to complex 3. However, complex 1 has the highest hydrophobicity in the series, which is probably due to the –OCH2CH3 group (in the ligand skeleton), which may enhance the hydrophobicity of the complex.

Octanol-Water Partition Coefficients. This experiment was accomplished according to a published literature method.47 1 mg sample of Mn-EDTA-EOB complex was dissolved in 2 mL of water and 1-octanol mixture (1:1 v/v). Resulting mixture was shaken for a second, then the vial was gently mixed on a rotator for 48 h. The mixture was then placed on the desk and allowed to be divided into two layers for 24 h at room temperature. Mn concentrations of each layer were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Octanol-water partition coefficients were computed using the equation log P = log(Co/Cw), where log P is the common logarithm of the partition coefficient, Co and Cw are the concentration of Mn in the 1octanol layer and water layer, respectively.

The water/n-octanol distribution coefficients were determined by the stir-flask method [39], [40]. Solutions of water-saturated octanol and octanol-saturated water were prepared by shaking equal volumes of octanol and water for one week and allowing the mixture to separate into the respective phases. An UV–Vis calibration curve was prepared for each complex in octanol-saturated water in a range 2–50 μM. A mixture of 10 mL n-octanol and 10 mL water (each saturated in the other) was stirred for 2 h at 37 °C, after adding the sample to be analyzed. The pH was maintained at 7.2 (5 mM Trizma-HCl). Once equilibrium was reached, the organic and aqueous phases were separated and centrifuged. Finally, the drug concentration in each phase was measured spectrophotometrically to determine values for P, [drug in octanol]/[drug in water]. Experiments were carried out three times [41] and the results expressed as Log P.

Reported log P is defined as log[complex]oct/[complex]wat. Final values were reported as the mean of three determinations.

Equal volumes of octanol and NaCl-saturated water were stirred at room temperature for 24 hours, and separated to give octanol-saturated water and water-saturated octanol. Five standard concentrations (5, 10, 20, 40 and 60 µM) of the complexes were prepared from the octanol-saturated water. Analysis using UV/vis spectroscopy was used to obtain a calibration curve of absorbance vs. concentration for each complex at its maximum absorbance. Accurate amounts of the complexes were dissolved in the octanol-saturated water (25 mL) to make up a concentration of 50 µM. 3 mL of octanol-saturated water containing the complex was placed in a centrifuge tube and 3 mL of water-saturated octanol was layered on top. Six samples prepared in this manner were shaken for 4 hours using a vibrax machine at 500 g min-1 . The layers were separated and the octanol-saturated water layer was retained for analysis using UV/vis spectroscopy. The average concentration of the six runs was calculated using the calibration graph and maximum absorbance for each complex. Subtraction of the average concentration obtained from the concentration of an unshaken sample in octanol-saturated water gave the final [C]org. The [C]org and [C]aq. were used to determine the partition coefficient log P.

The lipophilicity of the complexes was measured by determining their partition coefficients (log Po/w) between n-octanol (o) and water (w) using the shake-flask method. 8 A calibration plot for the complex was constructed by determining the absorbances by varying concentrations of the complex in the aqueous medium. The remaining concentration of the complex in the aqueous phase was then determined from the calibration plot. The partition coefficient was calculated by using the equation log Po/w = log[C]o/[C]w, where [C]o is the concentration of the complex in the n-octanol phase and [C]W is the concentration in the aqueous phase.

The lipophilicity of a compound is an important factor in determining ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination, and toxicology) properties of drug substances. These properties impact drug distribution across the tissues and are measured by the octanol/water partition coefficient (log P values).42 The log P values of the complexes were determined using 2% DMSO–H2O with n-octanol. The partition coefficient P was determined by the ratio of a compound's concentration in the organic phase (octanol) to the concentration of the compound in the aqueous phase (water). The average log P values of the complexes [Co(III)-dione] and [Co(III)-dox] were 0.89 and 0.55, respectively, suggesting a relatively hydrophilic nature favouring solubility in the bloodstream.

The octanol-water partition coefficients were determined as follows. Water (500 mL, distilled after MilliQ purification) and n-octanol (500 mL) were shaken together for 72 h to allow saturation of both phases (one week for the full separation of the two phases). Approximately 0.5 mg of the complexes were placed into a Falcon tube, and 2 mL of octanol-saturated water and 2 mL of water-saturated octanol were added into the same Falcon of the compound and shacked until the complexes were fully dissolved and divided into the two phases. Biphasic solutions were mixed for ten minutes and then centrifuged for five minutes at 6000 rpm to allow separation. Two aliquots of 500 μL for both phases were placed into metal-free PE tubes and 4 mL of a solution of HNO3Suprapure (dilution 1:1 with MilliQ water) for Ag and Au complexes, or 4 mL of 3HCl : HNO3 (aqua regia) solution Suprapure (dilution 1:1 with MilliQ water) for CDDP, were added to the aliquots to obtain 4 samples for each complex (2 for the water phase and 2 for the octanol phase). The solutions were mineralised at 90 °C overnight and 1.5 mL of MilliQ water were added at the end to have a final volume of 6 mL for each sample. The metal concentration in both phases was determined by ICP-OES.61,62

(11,58) Deionized water and 1-octanol were vigorously stirred for 24 h, to enable saturation of both phases, then separated by centrifugation. An aliquot of the solution (Vaq = 1.2 mL) was transferred into a test tube and water-saturated octanol (Vorg = Vaq = 1.2 mL) was added. The mixture was vigorously stirred for 20 min at 21 °C then centrifuged (5000 rpm, 5 min). The UV–vis spectrum of the aqueous phase was recorded (𝐴faq) and the partition coefficient was calculated as 𝑃𝑜𝑤=(𝐴0aq-𝐴faq)/𝐴faq Pow = (A0aq - Afaq)/Afaq, where 𝐴0aq and 𝐴faq are the absorbance in the aqueous phase before and after partition with the organic phase, respectively.30c The wavelength of the maximum absorption of each compound (280–380 nm range) was used for UV–vis quantitation. The procedure was repeated three times for each sample (from the same stock solution); results are given as mean ± standard deviation (Table 1). Octanol-saturated water (OSW) and water-saturated octanol (WSO) were prepared from octanol and 0.2 M water solution of KCl (to suppress possible hydrolysis) by overnight stirring. The stock solution was prepared by shaking of 1 mmol of complex 1 in 11 mL of OSW for 1 h. Then the mixture was centrifuged (5 min, 11,000 rpm) and the supernatant was collected. 5 mL of the supernatant was studied by ICP-MS (to assess [1]OSWb as the Ir concentration before partition), while other 5 mL of the supernatant was added to 5 mL of WSO and shaken for 2 h at ambient temperature. After that, this mixture was centrifuged, and the aqueous layer was carefully separated. The Ir concentrations were determined by ICP-MS (the obtained value was corrected for the adsorption effects; see above). The equation log P = log([M]WSO/[M]OSWa) was used for the partition coefficient calculation, where [M]OSWa stands for the Ir concentration after partition, and [M]WSO = [M]OSWb – [M]OSWa. The experiment was conducted in triplicate and the results are presented as arithmetic mean ± SD.

The distribution coefficient values (D7.4) of the compounds were determined by the traditional shake-flask method in n-octanol/buffered aqueous solution at pH 7.40 for 5 mM Tris HCl with 0.1 M KCl and at pH 7.4 at 25.0 ± 0.2 °C. The ligand and complexes were dissolved in n-octanol (presaturated by the aqueous buffer) because of the very low aqueous solubility. The aqueous buffer solution and n-octanol ratio was 1:1 due to the expected high lipophilicity of the compounds. First, samples were mixed with vertical rotation (∼20 rpm) for 3 h, and then the two phases were separated by centrifugation at 3000 rpm (∼1000g) for 3 min. After separation, UV–vis spectra of the compounds were recorded in both phases. Spectra of the n-octanol phases were compared to those of the original n-octanol stock solutions. The distribution coefficient values were also determined using unbuffered water and octanol (also presaturated) with a ratio of 1:1.

Different ratios (v/v, 0.5:1, 1:1, and 2:1) of the saturated solutions were shaken with presaturated n-octanol for 20 min on an orbital shaker to obtain the partition coefficient.

The octanol-water partition coefficients were determined as follows. Water (500 cm3, distilled after MilliQ purification) and n-octanol (500 cm3) were shaken together for 72 h to allow saturation of both phases (one week for the full separation of the two phases). Approximately 0.5 mg of the complexes were placed into a Falcon tube, and 2.0 cm3 of octanol-saturated water and 2.0 cm3 of water-saturated octanol were added into the same Falcon of the compound and shacked until the complexes were fully dissolved and divided into the two phases. Biphasic solutions were mixed for ten minutes and then centrifuged for five minutes at 6000 rpm to allow separation. Two aliquots of 0.50 cm3 for both phases were placed into metal-free PE tubes and 4.0 cm3 of 3HCl: HNO3 (aqua regia) solution Suprapure (dilution 1:1 with MilliQ water) were added to the aliquots to obtain 4 samples for each complex (2 for the water phase and 2 for the octanol phase). The solutions were mineralised at 90 °C overnight and 1.5 cm3 of MilliQ water were added at the end to have a final volume of 6.0 cm3 for each sample. Concentrations of both phases were determined by ICP-OES.

Partition coefficients for the platinum complexes were determined in triplicate in an n-octanol/water system, with different ratios (1:1, 1:2, 2:1). Each complex was dissolved in n-octanol at the concentrations 16.7, 12.5, or 10 μM and subsequently, an appropriate volume of water was added. The mixtures were shaken mechanically for 1 h to ensure the distribution between the two solvent phases. The samples were then centrifuged (13,000 rpm, 10 min). Afterwards, the platinum concentration was determined in the octanol phases by UV–vis spectrophotometry, after collecting a calibration line for each complex. Results are expressed as the logarithm of the partition coefficient of octanol/water (log Po/w), which is the logarithm of the concentration of platinum in the n-octanol divided by its concentration in the aqueous layer.

Results are expressed as the logarithm of the partition coefficient of octanol/water (log Po/w), which is the logarithm of the concentration of platinum in the n-octanol divided by its concentration in the aqueous layer.

To determine the LogP for the gold(III) dithiocarbamate complexes, a stock solution (1000 μM) was prepared in acetonitrile. In a 1.5 mL Eppendorf tube was added 400 μL of presaturated octanol, 400 μL of DI water, and 200 μL of the test sample was added. The sample was agitated for 30 min and centrifuged at 10,000 g at 23 °C for 15 min, and the octanol layer was separated from the water layer. HPLC trace of each layer was taken, and the partition coefficient of the complexes in a presaturated octanol–water solution was determined by measuring their affinity to each phase. The log absorbance of the HPLC trace of each phase was measured and calculated using: logP = (absorbance of octanol layer) / (absorbance of water layer)

The log Po/w of the prepared complexes (Ru2L1, Ir2L1, Re2L1, Ru2L2, Ir2L2, and Re2L2) were determined by dint of shake flask method using the previously published procedure. A known amount of each complex was suspended in water (pre-saturated with n-octanol) and shaken for 48 h on an orbital shaker. To permit phase separation, the solution was centrifuged for 10 min at 3000 rpm. To get the partition coefficient, different ratios (1:2, 1:1, and 2:1) of the saturated solutions were shaken with pre-saturated n-octanol for 20 min on an orbital shaker and followed the same procedure. Aliquots of the aqueous and octanol layers were pipetted out separately and the absorbance was measured with a UV-Vis spectrophotometer using proper dilution. The partition coefficient (log Po/w) values were obtained from the ratio of absorbance value.

The lipophilicity of the metal complex was determined by measuring its distribution coefficient between the phosphate-buffered saline and octanol phase by using the “shake-flask” method. For this technique, the phases used were previously saturated with each other. The complex was dissolved in phase (A) with its major presence with an absorbance of about 0.5 at 350 nm. This solution was then mixed with an equal volume of the other phase (B) at 300 rpm for 12 h and then equilibrated overnight. Phase A was then carefully separated from phase B. The amount of the complex before and after the sample mixing was determined by UV/vis absorption spectroscopy at 350 nm using a Jasco V-670 spectrophotometer. The evaluation of the complexes was repeated three times, and the ratio between the organic and aqueous phase was calculated.

The lipophilicity of the gallium complexes was determined as the octanol/PBS distribution coefficient at pH 7.4 (LogD7.4) using a shake-flask procedure. PBS (pH 7.4) and n-octanol were mutually pre-saturated by shaking at 180 rpm and 37 °C overnight to generate octanol-saturated PBS (OSP) and PBS-saturated octanol (PSO). Calibration curves were obtained by recording the UV–vis absorbance of a series of solutions (0–32 μg mL-1) prepared in OSP or PSO. For partitioning, 2 mg of each gallium complex was added to a mixture of PBS (5 mL) and octanol (5 mL), shaken at 180 rpm and 37 °C for 12 h, then centrifuged to ensure phase separation. The absorbance of the compounds in the octanol and PBS layers was measured and converted to concentration using the corresponding standard curves and calculation. LogD7.4 = log10(Coctanol / CPBS)

The shake flask method was applied to measure the lipophilicity of 5FU-gallium corrole conjugates with a UV–vis spectrometer. First, the corrole complexes at different concentrations were prepared in 1-octanol presaturated with PBS (10×, pH 7.4). Then, equal volumes of the PBS presaturated with 1-octanol were added and mixed. The resulting solution was placed in a homoiothermic (25 °C) shaker at 200 rpm for 4 h. After the oil and water distribution achieved equilibrium, the concentration of corrole complexes in the oil layer was obtained by analyzing UV–vis absorption spectra. The octanol/water partition coefficient log PO/W (Po/w = Co/Cw = Ao/Aw, where A represents absorbance) of 5FU-gallium corrole conjugates was calculated by eq 1: (67-69) log𝑃o/w=log{(𝐶o)final/[(𝐶o)initial-(𝐶o)final]}

The lipophilicity of each complex was determined via a standard shake-flask method, and is expressed as a log (Po/w) value where Po/w represents the octanol/water partitioning coefficient. To determine the log (Po/w) value of each complex, complexes were dissolved into 1000 μL of ultra-purified water saturated octanol, followed by the addition of 1000 μL of ultra-purified water saturated with octanol. The layers were thoroughly agitated by vortexing for 30 s. The mixtures were placed into a 37 °C incubator with shaking for 24 h before the layers were separated, and the interface discarded. These were then aliquoted into 2–3 % nitric acid with the indium content in each analysed via ICP-OES or ICP-MS. These values were then taken and used to calculate the log (Po/w). All log (Po/w) analyses were performed in triplicate.

The partition coefficients of the complexes in octanol and water were determined using previously reported methods [S5]. Octanol–saturated water and water–saturated octanol were prepared by stirring the mixture for 24 h. Aliquots of stock solutions of the complexes 1-6 in octanol–saturated water (2 mL) were added to the same volumes of water–saturated octanol (2 mL) and shaken in a Tarsons rotospin test tube mixer at a speed of 50 rpm min-1 for 24 h. The absorbance values of the equilibrated layers and the blanks are read at the absorption maxima ~280 nm, and the partition coefficient is calculated with the equation:log P = log[([A]org - [A]blank) / ([A]aq - [A]blank)] ... (2)where, [A]org, [A]aq and [A]blank are the absorbance of the organic layer, aqueous layer and the blank, respectively.

The lipophilicity of the radiocomplexes was evaluated by the “shake-flask” method [75]. Briefly, the radioactive complexes were added to a mixture of octanol (1 mL) and 0.1 M PBS pH 7.4 (1 mL), previously saturated in each other. This mixture was vortexed and centrifuged (3000 rpm, 10 min, RT) to allow phase separation. Four aliquots of both octanol and PBS were counted in a gamma counter. The octanol-water partition coefficients were calculated by dividing the counts in the octanol phase by those in the buffer. The results expressed as log D7.4 are presented in Table 5.

The partition coefficients of 1–4 were determined at three different concentrations and averaged out.

The octanol–water distribution coefficients of all the ruthenium compounds were determined at pH 7.4 by employing the shake-flask procedure [46]. The obtained results, expressed as logarithm values logD7.4, are shown in Table 2. Briefly, aqueous solutions of the tested compounds (16 μM) buffered with phosphate buffer at pH 7.4 were mixed in a flask with n-octanol. Both solvents were mutually pre-saturated at room temperature. The compounds were then allowed to equilibrate between the organic and the aqueous media by flask handshaking and then were left resting for at least 24 h to ensure the complete separation of the two phases. Afterwards, the concentrations of ruthenium compounds in the aqueous phase were spectrophotometrically determined while those in the organic phase were obtained by difference. The logD7.4 values were calculated by using the Eq. 2: logD7.4(S) = log(Coctanol / Cwater) = log((mO × VW) / (mW × VO)) where S stands for the sample (ruthenium compounds) analysed, COctanol and CWater represent the total concentration of the compound in the organic and in the aqueous phase, m stands for the mass of compound in the aqueous (w) or in the organic phase (o) and V was the volume of each phase. A ligand concentration of 15 μM was used while different Vw/Vo ratios were employed, varying from 0.5:1 to 2:1. Each determination was performed in triplicate. Because of the ionizable nature of compounds herein analysed, we referred to distribution coefficients (D) instead of partition coefficients (P). In fact, differently from logP, which can be used to characterize the octanol-water partition of a compound in its neutral/uncharged form, logD7.4 more adequately describes the distribution of a compound that can be partially ionized at a given pH value.

Partition coefficients of the complexes were determined in duplicate in an n-octanol/water system. Each complex was dissolved in 1.5 mL of water at 7 × 10- 5 M and subsequently an equal volume of n-octanol was added. The mixtures were shaken mechanically for 24 h to assure the distribution between the two solvent phases. The samples were centrifuged (13,000 rpm for 5 min). Afterwards, they were diluted 50-fold and the copper concentration was determined in both phases by graphite furnace atomic absorption spectrometry (GFAAS) in a Varian model Zeeman AA 240 spectrophotometer equipped with a graphite tube atomizer and an autosampler. Results are expressed as apparent partition coefficients (P), which were determined from the total metal concentration in n-octanol divided by the total metal concentration in the aqueous layer.

The lipophilicity of our compounds, i.e. their partition coefficient in an n-octanol/water system, was measured using the shake-flask method [30], [31]. To suppress hydrolysis of the chloride ligands a 0.15 M NaCl buffer served as a water phase. The coefficients (logP) were expressed as the log10 of the ratio of the compound concentration in the n-octanol phase to the compound concentration in the aqueous phase. The mixture of the abovementioned solutions in ratio 1:1 was shaken mechanically for 24 h. All the measurements were executed only in n-octanol solution as none of tested compounds 3–5 was soluble in the used buffer. Then, the amount of compound in water phase was estimated as the difference between the absorbance of the compound in n-octanol and the absorbance of this sample after stirring it with water solution. The amount of compounds in n-octanol phase after stirring was determined by UV–vis spectroscopy on a Varian Bio 100 UV–vis spectrophotometer. The partition coefficients were expressed as the log10 of the ratio of the compound concentration in the n-octanol layer to the compound concentration in the aqueous layer. All measurements were executed at least seven times. Equal volumes (1 mL) of the aqueous solution and n-octanol were shaken together mechanically for 24 h.

The D values of l- and d-Pro-FTSC and their copper(II) complexes were determined by the traditional shake-flask method in an n-octanol/buffered aqueous solution at pH 7.4 (HEPES buffer) at 298.0 ± 0.2 K as described previously. (32, 33) Two parallel experiments were performed for each sample. The ligands were dissolved at 1.0 × 10–4 M and the complexes at 1.0 × 10–4 M in the n-octanol presaturated aqueous solution of the buffer (0.02 M) at a constant ionic strength (0.10 M KCl). The aqueous solutions and n-octanol with a 1:1 phase ratio were gently mixed with 360° vertical rotation for 3 h to avoid the emulsion formation, and the mixtures were centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 3 min by a temperature-controlled centrifuge (Sanyo) at 298 K. After separation, UV–vis spectra of the ligands or complexes in the aqueous phase were compared to those of the original aqueous solutions. Because no measurable amount of the ligands or the copper(II) complexes was found in the n-octanol phase, D7.4 values were merely estimated.

The partition coefficient for the copper (II) complexes was determined in duplicate in an n-octanol/water system at pH 7.4. An emulsion of equal volumes (1500 μL) of an aqueous solution of the copper complex (6.7 × 10-4 mol L-1) and n-octanol was prepared. The system containing the mixture was hermetically sealed, protected from light, and kept under vigorous and continuously shaking for 24 h. The mixture was centrifuged (13000 rpm, 10 min) and aliquots of both phases were carefully taken from the top n-octanol and the bottom aqueous layers. Copper concentration in both aqueous and n-octanol layers was determined by GFAAS in a Varian model Zeeman 220 spectrophotometer equipped with a graphite tube atomizer and an autosampler. The partition coefficient was expressed as log P, in which P = [Cu]n-octanol/[Cu]aqueous.

The lipophilicity of complexes 1–3 was determined by calculating the partition coefficient, P (or log Kow). It is determined by the shake-flask method, which gives an idea of the relative distribution of the complexes between 1-octanol and water. Herein, we have used 1-octanol as a mimic of the hydrophobic bilayer. Briefly, 1 mg of the complexes was mixed with water (5 mL) presaturated with 1-octanol. The UV-vis absorption spectra of the solution were recorded to obtain Ai. Then the mixture was treated with 1-octanol presaturated with water and the layers were separated. The spectrum of the aqueous layer was recorded to get Af. The equilibrium constant, Kow, was obtained using the equation: Kow = ((AiDFi - AfDFf)Vwater) / (AfDFfVoctanol) DFi and DFf are the dilution factors used to obtain Ai and Af respectively. Vwater and Voctanol are the volumes of the water and octanol phases.

The water/n-octanol distribution coefficients were determined by the stir-flask method [22], [23]; water-saturated n-octanol and n-octanol-saturated water were prepared by shaking equal volumes of n-octanol and water for one week and allowing the mixture to separate into the respective phases. A UV–visible (UV–vis) calibration curve for each complex in n-octanol-saturated water in the 2–50 μM range was prepared. A mixture of 10 mL n-octanol and 10 mL water (each saturated in the other) was stirred for 1 h at 37 °C, after adding the sample to be analysed. Once equilibrium was reached, the organic and aqueous phases were separated and centrifuged. Finally, the concentration of drug in each phase was measured spectrophotometrically to determine values for Log P = Log [drug in n-octanol]/[drug in water]. Experiments were carried out three times [24].

As non-substituted copper pyrithione complex has very poor solubility in water, determiningthe extinction coefficient of this complex in water is highly inefficient. Therefore, anothertechnique, ICP-OES analysis was utilised to measure concentrations of copper in each layer.In this process, sample preparation for each complex followed everything similar as that forshake-flask method until UV measurement. After separating the two solvent layers, samplesfor measuring copper concentrations in octanol and water layer were prepared differently. Forthe octanol layer, 100 μl was collected in a vial and the solvent was evaporated under highvacuum. Lipophilicity (log P) was determined for complex [Cu(ttpy)2]Cl2 between n-octanol and water phases using the shake-flask method. The phases of water-saturated octanol and octanol-saturated water were prepared by stirring with equal volumes of water and octanol for 24 h. The complex, [Cu(ttpy)2]Cl2, (1 mg) was dissolved in octanol-saturated water and then mixed with water-saturated octanol and stirred at room temperature for 6 h. Then, the organic and aqueous phases were separated and centrifuged at 12000 rpm for 30 min. Finally, the concentration of the complex in both phases was measured by UV–Vis absorption spectroscopy to determine values for log P using the following equation: [Drug in octanol] / [Drug in water]

The log P values of the compounds were determined using the shake flask method.61 Water or phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) was stirred with octanol for 24 h, and then the mixture was centrifuged for 5 min to obtain octanol-saturated water and water-saturated octanol. 1–3 were dissolved in the octanolsaturated water (or PBS for cisplatin) at a typical concentration of 0.05 to 5 mM, and then they were mixed with water-saturated octanol in volumetric ratios of 1 : 1, 1 : 2, and 2 : 1. All mixtures were prepared in duplicate. The mixtures were vortexed for 0.5 h, and then they were centrifuged for 5 min. The layers were separated carefully using a fine-gauge needle. The copper content in the layers was analyzed using graphite furnace atomic absorption spectroscopy (GFAAS). The partition coefficient was taken as the ratio of the concentration of copper in the octanol layer to that in the aqueous layer (P = coct/cwater). The reported error is the standard deviation of triplicate measurements obtained according to this protocol.

Partition coefficients were measured using PBS and 1-octanol as described by Green, et al. [8], [9] using a small aliquot (typically 20 μL) of the product and 5 mL each of PBS and 1-octanol. Partition coefficient of the complexes in octanol–water system was determined using standard shake-flask method.52 Octanol and water (equal volume) were pre-equilibrated overnight before the experiment.53 After equilibration the solid samples were added to the mixture of solvents and shaken on a dancing shaker overnight at room temperature. On the next day the tubes were centrifuged and left undisturbed for an hour. Aliquots of the aqueous and octanol layers were pipetted out separately and the absorbance measured using UV-vis spectroscopy. Concentration of the substances in each layer was calculated using the respective molar extinction coefficients of 1–3.

The partition coefficient was calculated as a ratio of counts in the octanol fraction to counts in the PBS fraction.

Information about the lipophilicity of the 64Cu-labelled cyclam propionic acid ligands was obtained by using water/1-octanol mixtures. The experiments were performed with 100 μM solutions of cyclam propionic acid ligands dissolved in 1-octanol. The aqueous phases consisted of 0.05 M HEPES/NaOH buffer (440 μL; pH 7.2, 7.4 or 7.6), [64Cu]CuCl2 solution (10 μL, 500 kBq), and a 100 μM Cu(NO3)2 solution (50 μL). The distribution experiments were performed at (25 ± 1) °C in microcentrifuge tubes (2 cm3) with mechanical shaking for 30 min. The phase ratio V(1-octanol)/V(aq) was 1:1 (0.5 mL each). Full complexation was checked by radio-HPLC, which provided no evidence of free copper(II) species in the aqueous phase. All samples were centrifuged, and the phases were then separated. The concentration of the copper complex in both phases was determined radiometrically by using γ radiation [64Cu, NaI(Tl) scintillation counter automatic γ counter 1480, Wizard 3″, Perkin–Elmer]. The results are the average values of three independent experiments.

For n-octanol/water partition coefficient (LogP) measurements, a weighted amount of a selected metal-DTC complex (ca. 1 mg) was dissolved in n-octanol (20 mL), previously pre-saturated with deionized water for 24 hours. The obtained solution was shaken for 2 hours in the presence of 20 mL of deionized water at 25 °C and, subsequently, the mixture was left to equilibrate for 30 minutes. The concentration of every metal-DTC derivative in the n-octanol phase before (C0) and after partitioning (C1) was measured by UV-Vis spectrophotometry, followed by the evaluation of the corresponding LogP = log (C1)/(C0-C1)31.

The log P values copper(II) complexes and ligands were determined according to the shake-flask method [23]. Weighted amounts of the analyzed compounds were partitioned between equal volumes of water and 1-octanol by shaking for 3 h at room temperature. Due to low solubility of copper(II) complexes, the shaking time was elongated to 24 h to assure full partitioning of the analyzed compounds between two water and 1-octanol phases. Then, the solution was centrifuged at 3500g (15 min) for separate into two layers. The concentration of Cu(II) complexes and ligands in the aqueous phase were measured by UV/VIS spectrometry. Additionally for ligands, both phases were analyzed by HPLC method in isocratic elution (80% methanol in water). Each sample (separated phase) was injected into C18 reversed-phase column and the peak area was determined. On the basis of these results, the partition coefficients were calculated.

A modified shake-flask method was used to determine the partition coefficients of the complexes 1–6 between n-octanol and water.41 Briefly, 5 ml solution of a complex in octanol-saturated water was shaken with 5 ml of water-saturated n-octanol in a falcon tube for ∼30 min using a vortex. The biphasic mixture was centrifuged for ∼5 min at 4000 rpm and the layers were separated. The concentration of the complexes 1–6 in each layer was measured by UV-visible spectroscopy. The partition coefficients of 1–6 were determined at three different concentrations and averaged out.

The lipophilicity was calculated as the average log ratio value of the radioactivity in the organic fraction and the PBS fraction from the 6 samples.

Hydrophobicity was evaluated by measurement of distribution ratio (D) in the 1-octanol/water system using the shake flask method. A MOPS buffer 10-2 M pH = 7.40 ± 0.02 was employed as aqueous phase. Both phases, organic and aqueous, were presaturated with 10-4 M of each test complex, then the UV spectrum (Agilent 8453 spectrophotometer) was recorded for each phase before placing them together in a 8 ml vial carefully degreased. The vial was shaken vigorously inside a water bath with constant temperature T = 25.0 ± 0.5 °C, protected from light for 3 h. At the end of the incubation, the mixture was centrifuged for 10 min at 3000 rpm to break the emulsion, the layers were separated with a Pasteur pipette, and concentrations in both phases were measured by electronic absorption spectroscopy in the UV region at the second band of absorption around 290 nm. The wavelengths used for each complex and their molar extinction coefficient are reported in Table 1. The test was done by triplicate and D was calculated as the average concentration ratio Co/Cw, where Co is the final concentration in the organic phase and Cw is the final concentration in the aqueous phase.

Partition coefficients (log P) of Cu(II) Schiff base ligand and complexes were determined by spectroscopy method. Octanolsaturated water (OSW) and water-saturated octanol were prepared using analytical grade actanol and milli-Q water. Aliquots of stock solutions of ligand and copper complexes in OSW were added to equal volumes of WSO and shaken in an Eppendorf ThermoMixer C shaker for 24 h at 250 rpm after partition. The aqueous and octanol layers were carefully separated into test tubes for copper analysis. Aqueous samples before and after partitioning were analysed by spectroscopy method calibrated with aqueous standards. Partition coefficients of compounds were calculated using the equation log Poct = log ([compound]oct / [compound]aq).

The lipophilicity of the complexes, which was presented as Log Po/w values, was determined via the shake-flask method. Log Po/w is defined as the logarithmic ratio of complexes in n-octanol to that in the aqueous phase. To a centrifuge tube, add 1 mL of "n-octanol-saturated aqueous phase" (adjusted to the target pH) and 1 mL of "water-saturated n-octanol phase". All drugs have been prepared as 10 mM solutions in DMSO as stock drug solution. Following equilibrium via shaking (40 μM), the centrifuge tube is centrifuged at 3000–5000 rpm for 10–15 min to thoroughly disrupt the emulsion layer. The n-octanol and aqueous phases are then separately withdrawn, and its absorbance is measured. Calculations are performed using the Lambert-Beer law (A = εbc) and the formula Log Po/w = Log Coctanol/Cwater.

The lipophilicity of the metal complexes was determined by measuring its distribution coefficient between the and phosphate-buffered saline and Octanol phase by using the “shake-flask” method. For this technique, the used phases were previously saturated in each other. The complex was dissolved in the phase (A) with its major presence with an absorbance of about 0.5 at 350 nm. This solution was then mixed with an equal volume of the other phase (B) at 300 rpm for 12 h and then equilibrated overnight. The phase A was then carefully separated from phase B. The amount of the complex before and after the sample mixing was determined by UV/vis absorption spectroscopy at 350 nm using a Jasco V-670 spectrophotometer. The evaluation of the complexes was repeated three times and the ratio between the organic and aqueous phase calculated.

The lipophilicity of metal complexes may influence the cellular uptake efficiency and cytotoxicity, which is usually studied by the shake flask method. The lipophilic properties of the complexes were analyzed by ICP-MS. The lipophilicity is usually expressed by log Po/w, which is the partition coefficient of the complexes distribution between n-octanol and aqueous phase. Negative log Po/w means the complex is hydrophilic and positive log Po/w means the complex is lipophilic. According to the results, the log Po/w of complexes 1 and 3 had negative value of -0.37 ± 0.02 and - 0.19 ± 0.01, respectively, while the value of complex 2 has a positive value of 0.22 ± 0.02 (Table 1). Solvent and pH can affect the lipophilicity of drugs. The logarithm of the distribution coefficient of the compound at certain pH in an organic phase (such as octanol) and an aqueous phase (such as buffer solution) is Log D. With the use of octanol and PBS (pH 7.4), Log D7.4 of the complexes 1–3 were calculated (Table 1).
